# Incident Report: Malware Infection — 2024-08-15

## Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.8.15.133** |
| MAC address | **00:1c:bf:03:54:82** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-H8ALZBV** |
| Windows domain | LAFONTAINEBLEU (AD domain, DC: WIN-JEGJIX7Q9RS.lafontainebleu.org) |
| Logged-in user | **plucero** (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString from 10.8.15.133) |

Host obtained its address via DHCP (offering hostname DESKTOP-H8ALZBV, MAC 00:1c:bf:03:54:82) from server 10.8.15.4, and was confirmed the same box via NBNS name registrations and repeated Kerberos traffic to the domain controller.

## Malware Family

**Latrodectus** loader (behavioral attribution — no IDS/Suricata alerts were included in the evidence set, so this is **not signature-confirmed**; it is based on infection-chain and traffic TTPs).

Supporting behavioral indicators:
- Delivery via a fake FedEx-invoice phishing page → ZIP → grossly oversized (6.99 MB) obfuscated `.js` downloader padded with irrelevant book/report text (a known evasion trick to inflate file size and dilute static-signature scanners), containing no visible malicious logic itself — consistent with a Latrodectus-style JS loader stage.
- The JS stage then used the legitimate Windows **BITS** service (User-Agent `Microsoft BITS/7.8`) to fetch a Windows PE32+ x86-64 DLL from a bare-IP HTTP host — a known Latrodectus second-stage retrieval technique (living-off-the-land download via `bitsadmin`/BITS COM API rather than the browser).
- Post-infection HTTP C2 beaconing to the same bare IP with a static, dated User-Agent (`Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 1.0.3705)`), issuing continuous GET/POST `/` requests roughly every 5–8 seconds for the rest of the capture (04:12–04:42, 30+ minutes), consistently answered with HTTP 400 — a beacon/check-in pattern typical of this loader family's C2 protocol.

## Indicators of Compromise

**Malicious domains**
- `quote.checkfedexexp.com` (initial phishing/redirect page, resolved to 104.21.55.70)
- `business.checkfedexexp.com` (secondary lookup, same phishing infrastructure)

**Malicious URL**
- `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215` — GET at 04:10:58, delivered the ZIP payload (104.21.55.70:80)

**Command-and-control endpoint**
- `72.5.43.29:80` — bare-IP HTTP host used both to serve the second-stage DLL and as the ongoing beacon destination

**Transferred files / hashes**
| File | Source | Size | SHA256 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js` (inside downloaded ZIP) | quote.checkfedexexp.com | 6,990,020 bytes | not separately hashed (ZIP container hash below) |
| ZIP container (delivered at the `/managements?...` URL) | 104.21.55.70 | 2,767,804 bytes | `798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc` |
| `0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` (Windows PE32+ x86-64 DLL, second-stage payload) | http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4 | 159,232 bytes | `b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6` |

**Timeline (approx., host local time in capture)**
- 04:09:45 — benign NCSI connectivity check (unrelated baseline traffic)
- 04:10:58 — GET to quote.checkfedexexp.com `/managements?...` → 2.7 MB ZIP delivered
- (ZIP contains the padded 7 MB JS downloader `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js`)
- 04:11:25–04:11:51 — Windows Update/BITS/Edge background traffic (legitimate, interleaved)
- 04:11:59–04:12:00 — `Microsoft BITS/7.8` HEAD/GET to `72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` → 159,232-byte DLL retrieved
- 04:13:00 onward through end of capture (~04:42) — periodic GET/POST beacons from 10.8.15.133 to `72.5.43.29:80` with the static old-style User-Agent, all answered HTTP 400 (C2 check-in loop)

## Recommendation
Isolate DESKTOP-H8ALZBV (10.8.15.133) from the network immediately, reset the `plucero` domain credentials, and block `72.5.43.29`, `quote.checkfedexexp.com`, and `business.checkfedexexp.com` at the perimeter/DNS. Preserve the host for forensic imaging before remediation, given evidence of a second-stage DLL payload already downloaded to disk.
